regions.label: Africa
regions.lede: Sub-Saharan and southern African species. Antivenom access is a genuine, ongoing logistical constraint across this region — several entries below flag current supply status rather than treating it as settled.

species.search: puff adder bitis arietans
species.title: Puff Adder
species.subtitle: Bitis arietans. The single most medically important snake across sub-Saharan Africa by case volume — widespread, common near human dwellings, and responsible for a large share of the region's estimated 314,000+ annual envenomings

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Rapid onset of pain and swelling at the bite site, progressing over hours. This is not a snake that hides its bite the way boomslang does — local findings are immediate and obvious.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Potently cytotoxic: severe pain, swelling, extensive blistering, and tissue necrosis at the bite site, which can leave patients vulnerable to serious secondary infection. Systemically, venom also has real hemotoxic activity — hypotension, spontaneous hemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy occur alongside the local picture, so don't anchor purely on "cytotoxic" and skip coagulation labs.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Immobilize the limb, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction. Given tissue destruction potential, minimize additional trauma to the bite site.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial limb measurements/marking as with other viper bites. Baseline and serial coagulation studies given the hemotoxic component. Aggressive wound care and low threshold for surgical consult given necrosis risk — this is one of the African species where secondary tissue infection is a real downstream threat, not just an antivenom question.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by SAIMR Polyvalent Snakebite Antiserum (South African Vaccine Producers), the regional gold standard, alongside gaboon adder, rinkhals, green/Jameson's/black mamba, and cape/forest/snouted/Mozambique spitting cobra. Recommended initial dose for serious cytotoxic bites (puff adder, gaboon adder) is 5–10 ampoules (50–100 mL) IV. A newer WHO-approved alternative, PANAF Polyvalent, covers 24 African species including puff adder but requires roughly double the volume for equivalent neutralization based on preclinical comparison data. SAIMR polyvalent has a real anaphylaxis rate — roughly 4 in 10 patients in some reporting — so treat only in a monitored setting with epinephrine ready.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for antivenom administration, wound care, and monitoring for compartment syndrome/secondary infection. Roughly 90% of hospitalized snakebite patients regionally don't end up needing antivenom — reserve it for progressive local or any systemic findings, not universally.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: SAIMR polyvalent antivenom supply is not a hypothetical concern — South Africa has had real, reported production shortages (most recently flagged in 2023–2024), and the product is also relied upon by neighboring countries with no domestic production of their own. Know your current regional supply chain before you need it, not during a shortage.

species.search: black mamba dendroaspis polylepis
species.title: Black Mamba
species.subtitle: Dendroaspis polylepis. Sub-Saharan Africa's most feared elapid — fast-moving, potently neurotoxic, capable of rapid progression to respiratory failure

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Neurotoxic signs can progress quickly relative to other elapids — this is not the slow-burn presentation seen with North American coral snake. Local findings at the bite are typically minimal, which can be falsely reassuring.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Classic descending neurotoxic pattern: ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, progressing to generalized paralysis and respiratory failure if untreated.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Rapid transport is the priority — this is one of the African species where time to definitive airway/antivenom access most directly determines outcome. Immobilize, remove constricting items, do not delay for field interventions that don't change outcome.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Airway equipment ready at bedside. Antivenom given in the acute phase of neurotoxic envenoming will often NOT halt progression of neurologic effects, especially respiratory paralysis already underway — the patient may still require ventilatory support regardless of antivenom timing, and will not survive without it if paralysis has already progressed.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by SAIMR Polyvalent. Recommended dose for neurotoxic bites (mambas, neurotoxic cobras) is 80–120 mL, up to 200 mL in severe mamba envenomation — meaningfully higher volume than the cytotoxic-bite dosing. A follow-up dose is occasionally required specifically in black mamba bites. Neurologic improvement after antivenom is often slow (2–6 hours) and can be unconvincing even when treatment is working — don't judge efficacy on a 30-minute window the way you might with a North American crotalid.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU-level care for any patient with bulbar or respiratory signs. Ventilator support may be needed independent of antivenom response.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Minimal bite-site findings with a confirmed or strongly suspected black mamba exposure is not reassurance — treat this like the North American coral snake principle: the wound doesn't tell you the story, the timeline does. Don't wait for antivenom response to commit to airway support if respiratory signs are progressing.

species.search: boomslang dispholidus typus vine snake twig snake colubrid
species.title: Boomslang
species.subtitle: Dispholidus typus. Afrikaans for "tree snake" — arboreal, shy, non-aggressive. Bites are rare and almost always occur during handling. Not covered by SAIMR Polyvalent — requires its own monovalent product

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: This is the single most dangerous timeline mismatch in African envenomation. Initial local findings at the bite are minimal — mild swelling or pain, sometimes nothing at all. Venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy (VICC) can appear within 4 hours but is classically delayed up to 72 hours. A patient can look and feel completely fine for a full day or more while coagulation factors are actively being consumed.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom metalloproteinases activate prothrombin and factors IX/X, driving a consumptive coagulopathy that depletes fibrinogen and platelets. Untreated, this progresses to frank DIC. Bleeding ranges from minor oozing at puncture sites and epistaxis/gum bleeding to life-threatening bleeding into muscle, hemoglobinuria with acute tubular necrosis, GI hemorrhage, and CNS bleeding.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Any confirmed or strongly suspected boomslang bite requires hospital evaluation regardless of how the patient looks — this cannot be cleared in the field or dismissed because the wound is unimpressive.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: The 20-minute whole blood clotting test (draw blood into a plain glass tube, leave undisturbed 20 minutes, check for clot formation) is a fast bedside screen used widely across African snakebite care when formal coag panels are slow to return. Serial coagulation studies are essential given the delayed timeline — a normal initial PT/PTT does not clear the patient. Point-of-care viscoelastic testing (ROTEM/TEG), where available, has been used to detect subclinical coagulopathy that standard labs missed.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: SAIMR Polyvalent does NOT cover boomslang — a separate SAIMR Boomslang monovalent antivenom (South African Vaccine Producers) is required, and its supply is even more limited and expensive (roughly R6,800/vial domestically, or cited as high as US$6,000/vial internationally) than the polyvalent product. Dose: 20 mL (2 ampoules) IV in isotonic fluid over 30 minutes; a follow-up 10 mL dose is sometimes needed. When given, it reliably normalizes coagulation factors. There is no cross-coverage from polyvalent antivenom — don't substitute it here.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit and monitor coagulation status for at least the full 72-hour window even if the patient is asymptomatic and initial labs are normal, given how delayed onset can be. Any confirmed bite warrants hospitalization on this basis alone.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The core teaching point: an unimpressive bite plus a real snake (or a plausible history of handling one) is not a benign combination here — it's the expected presentation before the coagulopathy declares itself. Confirm which antivenom your facility actually stocks; assuming polyvalent covers this species is a documented, repeated real-world error given the two products are so easily confused.

species.search: spitting cobra naja nigricollis naja mossambica naja pallida mozambique red spitting cobra black-necked cobra bite
species.title: Spitting Cobras — Bite
species.subtitle: Naja nigricollis (black-necked spitting cobra), N. mossambica (Mozambique spitting cobra), N. pallida (red spitting cobra), among others. This card covers the bite; venom spat into the eyes is a separate, non-critical problem — see the notice at the end of this page.

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling develop rapidly, similar in character to other cytotoxic African vipers/cobras, with potential for significant local tissue necrosis.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Predominantly cytotoxic: pain, swelling, blistering, and tissue destruction at the bite site. Systemic neurotoxicity is possible but the local tissue damage is usually the dominant clinical problem, distinguishing these from the primarily neurotoxic mambas.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard cytotoxic snakebite approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Standard cytotoxic snakebite wound care, monitoring for necrosis and secondary infection, serial limb assessment.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Mozambique spitting cobra is covered by SAIMR Polyvalent (dosed as for other cytotoxic bites, 5–10 ampoules). Black-necked spitting cobra (N. nigricollis) is covered by EchiTAb-Plus-ICP in West Africa alongside Echis and puff adder.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Managed per standard cytotoxic snakebite admission criteria — admit for antivenom, wound care, and necrosis/infection monitoring.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Confirm which antivenom product your facility stocks actually covers the specific Naja species in your area — coverage varies by product and region (SAIMR Polyvalent vs. EchiTAb-Plus-ICP), unlike the more uniform coverage for puff adder.

species.search: saw-scaled viper carpet viper echis ocellatus west african echitab
species.title: West African Carpet Viper (Saw-Scaled Viper)
species.subtitle: Echis ocellatus (and related Echis spp.). Small snake, huge burden — the single most important cause of snakebite death and disability across the West African savannah

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain, swelling, and bleeding from the bite site develop early. Systemic coagulopathy — the dominant threat — can be detected on bedside clotting tests within hours of a significant bite.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Systemic hemorrhage and incoagulable blood are the defining features: bleeding from the gums, nose, old wounds, and IV sites, with the potential for hemorrhagic shock, and occasional local tissue necrosis. This is the species responsible for the bulk of the region's snakebite mortality and morbidity — estimated incidence as high as ~500 per 100,000 population per year in some Nigerian savanna communities, with historically 10–20% of victims dying untreated.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Get the patient to a facility that can run a 20-minute whole blood clotting test and has antivenom on hand — in this region, that access question is often the actual determinant of survival, more than any specific field maneuver.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) is the primary bedside diagnostic tool used across West African snakebite care to confirm venom-induced coagulopathy when formal lab turnaround is too slow. Treat any confirmed incoagulable blood as an indication for antivenom.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Two purpose-built products developed specifically for this species given historic antivenom supply crises in the region: EchiTAb-G (MicroPharm, ovine, monospecific for E. ocellatus, initial dose 1 vial/10 mL) and EchiTAb-Plus-ICP (Instituto Clodomiro Picado, equine, covers E. ocellatus plus Naja nigricollis and Bitis arietans, initial dose 3 vials/30 mL). Head-to-head trial data: both restored blood clotting in the large majority of patients within 6 hours (76% EchiTAb-G, 83% EchiTAb-Plus-ICP in the pivotal trial), with EchiTAb-Plus-ICP slightly more effective but EchiTAb-G associated with fewer and less severe early reactions. Specific antivenom confers roughly 75% protection against death compared to no/inappropriate antivenom in meta-analysis, and mortality has more than doubled during periods when antivenom stocks ran out regionally — this is a supply chain issue with a directly measurable body count, not an abstraction.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit any patient with confirmed incoagulable blood for antivenom and serial coagulation monitoring. Pregnant patients have been successfully treated with EchiTAb IgG antivenom with good maternal outcomes when treatment isn't delayed — delayed presentation is the main driver of fetal loss, not the antivenom itself.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Antivenom raised against the Asian species Echis carinatus is NOT reliably effective against West African E. ocellatus — regional specificity matters here more than in most snakebite scenarios, and using the wrong product has been a documented real-world problem. Don't assume any "Echis antivenom" is interchangeable across regions.

species.search: thick-tailed scorpion fat-tail scorpion parabuthus southern african scorpion
species.title: Thick-Tailed (Fat-Tail) Scorpion
species.subtitle: Parabuthus spp. The medically significant scorpion genus across southern Africa, covered by a dedicated SAIMR antivenom

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Immediate significant pain at the sting site; systemic neurotoxic signs can follow within a similar timeframe to Centruroides envenomation in North America — faster progression and greater severity in children.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Neurotoxic picture: pain out of proportion to visible findings, potential for cranial nerve and neuromuscular dysfunction in significant envenomation, autonomic signs. Severity is greatest in young children and the elderly.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Analgesia, transport, lower threshold for urgency in pediatric patients.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Grade severity based on local vs. systemic/neurologic findings, similar framework to Centruroides grading. Supportive care (analgesia, benzodiazepines for agitation/neuromuscular symptoms) alongside antivenom decision-making.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: SAIMR Scorpion Antivenom (South African Vaccine Producers, equine) is produced specifically for Parabuthus species and is the regional product of record, produced by the same manufacturer as the SAIMR snake antivenoms.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Outpatient management for mild local envenomation; admit for systemic/neurologic signs, especially pediatric patients.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: As with Centruroides in North America, pediatric patients are disproportionately represented among severe envenomations — maintain a lower threshold for concern and antivenom consideration in children compared with adults presenting with the same sting history.

species.search: egyptian cobra naja haje
species.title: Egyptian Cobra
species.subtitle: Naja haje. One of Africa's largest true cobras, widespread across North and East Africa. Comparative toxicity studies rank its venom as considerably more lethal than the region's major vipers, consistent with the generally greater severity of cobra envenomation

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain develops promptly at the bite site; neurotoxic progression follows a similar descending pattern and timeline to other true cobras.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Combines significant neurotoxicity — ptosis, bulbar weakness, progressive descending paralysis — with real local cytotoxic tissue effects (swelling, blistering, potential necrosis) at the bite site, similar in character to the spitting cobra bite picture already covered on this page but from a non-spitting true cobra.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard elapid approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Given the potency profile, don't delay transport waiting to see how the local picture develops.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Airway readiness given real neurotoxic potential. Local wound care and monitoring for necrosis alongside the neurologic picture, the same dual-track approach used for the region's other cytotoxic-plus-neurotoxic cobras.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by SAIMR Polyvalent in southern/eastern parts of its range. In Egypt and neighboring North African countries, VACSERA polyvalent antivenom (Egypt) is the regional product, produced specifically against Naja haje, Cerastes cerastes, and other locally significant species — don't assume SAIMR is the only or default option across this species' full range; confirm which product is actually stocked regionally.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for airway monitoring and wound care per standard cytotoxic-plus-neurotoxic elapid protocol.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: This species spans a huge range across North and East Africa where antivenom supply chains genuinely differ by country — the product available in Egypt is not necessarily the same one stocked further south or east within this snake's range.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Spitting Cobra — Venom Ophthalmia
items.html: (eyes only, not a bite) — venom spat into the eyes causing burning pain, conjunctivitis, possible corneal erosion. Care: immediate copious irrigation (tap water/saline) is the entire treatment — no antivenom indicated; fluorescein exam and ophthalmology follow-up if corneal findings.

regions.label: Central & South America
regions.lede: Bothrops species cause the overwhelming majority of snakebite in this region, but three rarer entries here — bushmaster, coral snake, and the South American rattlesnake — each have a genuinely distinct clinical signature that changes management from the start.

species.search: fer-de-lance bothrops asper terciopelo lancehead
species.title: Fer-de-Lance
species.subtitle: Bothrops asper. Also called: terciopelo. The single most medically important snake across Central America and northern South America — responsible for the large majority of snakebites in the region it inhabits

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling develop rapidly and can progress aggressively over the following hours, with tissue destruction extending well beyond the immediate bite site in severe cases.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Severe local tissue damage — swelling, blistering, and necrosis, sometimes severe enough to threaten a limb — combined with systemic coagulopathy, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. This is a species where local destruction and systemic hemotoxicity both need active management, not just one or the other.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction — tissue destruction risk makes additional local trauma especially costly here.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial limb assessment and coagulation studies. Aggressive wound care and a low threshold for surgical consultation given the real risk of extensive local necrosis and secondary infection.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Regional polyvalent antivenoms are produced across multiple countries rather than a single continent-wide product — Instituto Clodomiro Picado (Costa Rica, PoliVal-ICP) for Central America, Instituto Bioclon (Mexico, Antivipmyn/Antivipmyn-Tri), Instituto Butantan (Brazil), and national institutes in Colombia and Peru, among others. Effectiveness varies by which regional Bothrops population a given product was raised against — this is another entry in the recurring theme of narrow geographic antivenom specificity, and it means "polyvalent" here still requires confirming the product matches the local venom population.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation monitoring, wound care, and surveillance for evolving necrosis or compartment syndrome.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Local tissue destruction can be severe enough on its own to threaten the limb even when systemic coagulopathy is well controlled — don't let a reassuring coagulation panel substitute for close wound surveillance. Confirm which regional antivenom product is stocked; this genus has real population-level venom variation across its range.

species.search: bushmaster lachesis muta lachesis acrochorda lachetic
species.title: Bushmaster
species.subtitle: Lachesis muta and L. acrochorda. The largest viper in the world. Bites are rare given the species' remote forest habitat, but carry disproportionately high mortality when they occur

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain, edema, and erythema develop similarly to a Bothrops bite, which is part of why this species is easy to misdiagnose early. The distinguishing systemic features — bradycardia, hypotension, diarrhea — can appear alongside the local picture rather than as a late finding.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom is necrotizing, hemorrhagic, myotoxic, and hemolytic, resembling Bothrops envenomation locally — but a distinct set of vagal/autonomic findings ("Lachesis syndrome") sets it apart: bradycardia, hypotension, diarrhea, vomiting, and blurred vision, thought to reflect a vagal or cholinergic venom effect not seen in other regional pit vipers. Severity is graded in part by the presence or absence of these vagal manifestations — their presence marks a severe envenomation.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach, with particular attention to reporting any bradycardia, diarrhea, or hypotension during transport — these findings should raise suspicion for this species over a more common Bothrops bite and shape which antivenom the receiving facility prepares.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: A documented, real diagnostic trap: because the local picture mimics Bothrops so closely, bushmaster bites have been misdiagnosed and treated with plain bothropic antivenom, delaying correct treatment — in one published case, this delay contributed to digit amputation and severe infection. Actively ask about and examine for the vagal symptom cluster in any pit-viper-pattern bite from bushmaster habitat.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: A dedicated lachetic antivenom has not been available since 1986 in some regions; current treatment relies on bothropic-lachetic combination antivenom (Brazil: Soro Antibotrópico-Laquético, Instituto Butantan) where available. Where a lachetic-specific or combination product isn't accessible, some published protocols describe using large volumes of Crotalidae polyvalent antivenom instead, reflecting how genuinely scarce dedicated product is for this rare species. Treatment is further complicated by the need for comparatively high doses even when appropriate antivenom is available.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation, cardiovascular, and wound monitoring. Given the misdiagnosis risk, reassess the working diagnosis if a "Bothrops bite" isn't responding as expected or shows vagal features.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Bradycardia and hypotension in a pit-viper-pattern bite from Central/South American forest habitat should raise bushmaster on the differential specifically — these findings run counter to the tachycardia/hypotension-from-hemorrhage pattern more typical of straightforward Bothrops envenomation, and getting the species right changes which antivenom is needed.

species.search: south american coral snake micrurus corallinus micrurus frontalis micrurus surinamensis
species.title: South American Coral Snake
species.subtitle: Micrurus corallinus, M. frontalis, and numerous other regional Micrurus species (genus spans ~80 species from the southern US to northern Argentina). Uncommon — roughly 1-2% of regional snakebites — but capable of rapid respiratory failure

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Follows the same deceptive pattern as the North American coral snake: local findings can be minimal, and neurotoxic onset is genuinely variable — one published case showed no neurotoxic signs until 14 hours after the bite, followed by respiratory failure requiring ventilation even after antivenom had been given.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Presynaptic and postsynaptic neuromuscular blockade producing progressive weakness, cranial nerve involvement, and descending paralysis that can culminate in respiratory failure and death by asphyxiation within 5-6 hours in severe untreated cases — though onset can also be markedly delayed, so a slow start doesn't guarantee a mild course.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Same principle as North American coral snake: an unimpressive bite from a confirmed or suspected elapid in this genus is not reassuring. Transport and monitor regardless of initial appearance.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Prolonged observation given the delayed-onset risk. Airway and ventilator readiness — published cases describe patients requiring multiple intubations and extended ventilatory support over several days even after appropriately timed antivenom.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Regional anti-elapidic antivenoms (Instituto Butantan in Brazil, national institutes elsewhere in the region) are raised against the more common local Micrurus species, but real species-level gaps exist — one well-documented case showed a standard Brazilian anti-elapidic antivenom unable to neutralize the lethal activity of a related Micrurus species despite venom similarity. Don't assume broad genus-level coverage; regional product selection matters as much here as with Echis or Bothrops.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU-level care for any patient with neurologic signs, with an expectation that recovery may take days and require ongoing ventilatory support.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Neither a benign-looking bite nor a slow initial course rules out a severe outcome with this genus — both the local exam and the early timeline can be falsely reassuring. This mirrors the North American coral snake and African black mamba pattern: elapid neurotoxicity often doesn't announce itself the way viper local tissue effects do.

species.search: brazilian wandering spider phoneutria armed spider banana spider
species.title: Brazilian Wandering Spider
species.subtitle: Phoneutria spp. Also called: armed spider, banana spider (for turning up in shipped banana crates). Severe systemic envenomation is uncommon (~3% of bites) but concentrates in young children and the elderly

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Immediate, severe local pain — often described as radiating — is the most consistent finding across essentially all bites. Systemic signs, when they occur, tend to develop over the following hour or so.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Local: intense pain, edema, erythema, sweating, and fasciculation at the site. Systemic (uncommon, ~3% of cases, concentrated in children under 10 and adults over 70): tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, sialorrhea, vomiting, tachypnea, and — a distinctive and well-documented finding — priapism. Shock and pulmonary edema are the rare severe complications, thought to relate to a surge in sympathetic activity.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Analgesia and transport, with lower threshold for urgency in young children and elderly patients specifically.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Most cases are managed symptomatically — local analgesia, ice. Reserve escalation for the systemic-sign subset, watching in particular for the cardiovascular and priapism findings that distinguish severe cases.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: A specific antivenom exists (produced regionally, including by Instituto Butantan) but is recommended only for patients who develop significant systemic manifestations — not for the large majority of bites, which are local-pain-only and self-limited with supportive care alone.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Outpatient management with analgesia for the typical local-only presentation. Admit and consider antivenom for systemic signs, especially in the two vulnerable age groups.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Priapism is a genuinely distinctive finding for this species among all the arachnids on this site — worth specifically asking about or noting in a male patient with systemic signs after a bite in this region. Don't reach for antivenom on pain alone; it's reserved for the systemic minority.

species.search: south american rattlesnake crotalus durissus terrificus cascavel crotoxin
species.title: South American Rattlesnake
species.subtitle: Crotalus durissus terrificus. Also called: cascavel (Brazil). Accounts for only about 10% of Brazilian snakebites but carries the highest case-fatality rate of any snake in the country — meaningfully more dangerous per-bite than the far more common Bothrops

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: This is the opposite presentation from Bothrops (fer-de-lance): local pain and swelling at the bite site are often minimal or absent, which can be falsely reassuring. The real damage is systemic and can take time to declare itself.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom is dominated by crotoxin, a potent presynaptic β-neurotoxin, producing neurotoxicity (ptosis, blurred vision, myasthenia-like weakness), systemic myotoxicity (myoglobinuria, elevated CK, risk of acute renal failure from rhabdomyolysis), and some hemotoxic/hemolytic activity. Reported mortality (roughly 1.1% in Brazilian series) exceeds that of the far more frequently encountered Bothrops species, despite the much lower bite volume — this is a species where rarity does not equal low risk.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Given how unimpressive the local bite can look, don't let a benign-appearing wound delay urgency — the systemic picture is what matters here.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Monitor for myotoxicity specifically — serial CK, urine myoglobin, and renal function — alongside the neurologic exam. In published pediatric case series, patients who received early, definitive antivenom therapy did well; the cases with major morbidity were specifically those where initial treatment was delayed or given by a suboptimal route (subcutaneous) before definitive IV antivenom followed later. Timing and route both matter.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Anti-crotalic antivenom (Instituto Butantan, Brazil, and other regional producers) is the specific regional product. Notably, a documented US case report of an escaped pet C. d. terrificus successfully treated the bite with CroFab — the standard North American product — when species-specific antivenom wasn't immediately available, based on crotoxin's structural and functional similarity to Mojave toxin (which CroFab is known to cover). This is a useful contingency fact for any exotic-pet exposure outside the snake's native range, though regional anti-crotalic antivenom remains the standard of care where available.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for neurologic, renal, and CK monitoring regardless of how mild the bite site appears. Given the documented morbidity difference between prompt IV antivenom and delayed/suboptimal-route treatment, don't let logistics substitute for getting definitive therapy started quickly.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The core teaching point mirrors this page's coral snake and boomslang entries: an unimpressive local bite does not mean a mild envenomation for this species — it's actually closer to the rule than the exception here, unlike Bothrops where local findings are the dominant early clue. Route and timing of antivenom administration have documented real-world consequences in pediatric case data — IV, and promptly.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: False Coral Snakes
items.html: (various non-venomous and mildly venomous mimics, e.g. Erythrolamprus and related genera) — banded coloration convincingly imitates true Micrurus coral snakes, causing significant alarm on sight alone. Care: species confirmation when possible; wound care only for a confirmed mimic bite, no antivenom or extended observation needed once true coral snake is excluded.

items.name: New World Tarantulas
items.html: (Theraphosidae, e.g. Goliath birdeater and related genera) — the bite itself is generally mild in humans despite the intimidating size of these spiders; the bigger irritant is often urticating hairs flicked defensively, causing skin and eye irritation rather than systemic envenomation. Care: tape-strip removal of hairs from skin, eye irrigation if ocular contact, analgesia for bite-site pain; no antivenom exists or is needed.

regions.label: Europe
regions.lede: The lowest-acuity region in this build overall, but "low-severity" is a population-level statement, not a guarantee for the patient in front of you — a genuine minority of European viper bites and false widow bites still need real intervention.

species.search: european adder vipera berus asp viper vipera aspis nose-horned viper vipera ammodytes horned viper sand viper
species.title: European Vipers
species.subtitle: Vipera berus (common European adder — the only venomous snake native to the UK), V. aspis (asp viper — France, Italy, Switzerland), and V. ammodytes (nose-horned viper — the Balkans, most dangerous of the three). One antivenom family covers all three, but severity differs meaningfully by species and geography

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling develop over the first hours. Most bites across this genus stay mild-to-moderate; a genuine minority progress to systemic involvement, and that minority is meaningfully larger and more severe for V. ammodytes than for V. berus.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Progressive local swelling, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, and — in more severe cases — acute kidney injury, hemorrhage, angioedema, pulmonary edema, and rarely cardiac arrest or neurotoxicity. V. ammodytes stands apart within the genus: in the largest published case series (Croatia, >500 confirmed bites), roughly 16-22% of victims developed local or systemic complications, with neurotoxic findings (ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia, dysphonia, neuromuscular weakness) in about 15-16% of cases — genuinely uncommon for a European viper but well short of rare. Fatalities from V. ammodytes are documented, though concentrated in children and hypersensitive individuals rather than typical healthy adults.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize the limb, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial limb assessment and monitoring for systemic signs. In the UK, decisions on antivenom are guided by the National Poison Information Service via TOXBASE rather than a fixed local protocol — involve regional poison control early given how genuinely uncommon these bites are for most clinicians to have direct experience with.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: ViperaTAb (MicroPharm, UK, ovine Fab, monospecific against V. berus) and Viperfav (MicroPharm/France, similar Fab product) both show cross-reactivity across European Vipera species in animal models and supporting clinical data, including published use for V. aspis and V. ammodytes envenomation. In UK audit data, 20-60 of an estimated 50-200 annual V. berus bites are treated with antivenom, given IV, with better outcomes reported for IV Fab products (ViperaTAb, Viperfav) compared with older intramuscular antivenoms (Zagreb, Biomed, Bulbio) still used in parts of continental Europe. A single IV dose of Viperfav has shown good efficacy and pharmacokinetics for V. ammodytes specifically when given within hours of the bite.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for observation and antivenom consideration per regional poison control guidance for any bite with progressive local swelling or systemic signs. Given the neurotoxic minority within V. ammodytes bites specifically, maintain a lower threshold for airway/respiratory monitoring with confirmed or suspected bites from that species and geography.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: "Low severity" describes the population, not the individual patient — a genuine subset of bites from any of these three species need real antivenom and monitoring, and V. ammodytes in particular should not be mentally filed alongside the milder V. berus. Older intramuscular antivenoms (Zagreb, Biomed, Bulbio) still in regional use have weaker outcome data than the newer IV Fab products — know which product your local supply chain actually carries.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Noble False Widow Spider
items.html: (Steatoda nobilis) — the only medically significant spider in the UK/Ireland, frequently sensationalized in local media as "flesh-eating." Confirmed case series show sharp local pain, erythema, and swelling resolving fully within 48-72 hours with no lasting complications; venom does share Latrodectus-like toxin components but at far lower potency than true widows. Care: analgesia, ice, wound hygiene; the rare reports of severe necrosis or sepsis are almost always secondary bacterial infection from a dirty wound, not the venom itself — clean the bite site and this risk drops accordingly.

items.name: European Scorpion
items.html: (Euscorpius spp.) — small, low-potency scorpions found across Southern Europe; sting severity is comparable to a bee sting for the overwhelming majority of cases. Care: ice, analgesia, reassurance; no antivenom exists or is needed.

regions.label: Marine (Global)
regions.lede: Grouped by mechanism rather than geography, since the species that matter cluster around the Indo-Pacific but the decontamination step you pick first — vinegar, hot water, or neither — is the single most consequential decision on this page and it varies dangerously by species.

species.search: box jellyfish chironex fleckeri cubozoan sea wasp
species.title: Box Jellyfish
species.subtitle: Chironex fleckeri. Also called: sea wasp. Widely described as the most venomous marine animal — a severe sting is one of the fastest-acting lethal envenomations known, with fatal cardiac arrest documented within 15-20 minutes

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Sudden, severe pain on contact. Stings covering more than roughly 10% of body surface area can progress to cardiorespiratory arrest within 5-10 minutes — this is described in the literature as among the most explosive envenomation processes known in humans. Most stings, however, are far less severe and respond to first aid alone.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Immediate severe pain with characteristic whip-like linear tentacle marks. Severe envenomation causes direct toxic effects on the myocardium and cell membranes broadly — myocardial irritability, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema, hypotension, and cardiac arrest, described as toxic rather than allergic in mechanism.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Douse generously with vinegar (4-6% acetic acid) to inactivate any undischarged nematocysts still on the skin — this does not relieve pain from venom already injected, but prevents further envenomation from adherent tentacles, which are present in roughly 30% of stings. If vinegar isn't available, diluted acidic alternatives (even cola) have been suggested, though effectiveness is debated; alcohol-based products must be avoided, as they trigger further nematocyst firing. Do NOT apply a pressure immobilization bandage — pressure itself can trigger nematocyst discharge and the venom acts too fast for PBI to meaningfully slow systemic spread. Begin CPR immediately for any cardiac arrest; vigorous, sustained resuscitation is explicitly the best prehospital survival factor for a massive sting.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Continue vinegar decontamination and remove remaining tentacles. Cardiorespiratory monitoring for any patient with significant sting area or pain refractory to first aid. IV magnesium sulfate has evidence for pain and cardiovascular control, particularly when response to antivenom is inadequate. Verapamil has been used in refractory circulatory arrest based on case data.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Box Jellyfish Antivenom (CSL, ovine) exists but its clinical effectiveness is genuinely disputed — animal studies conflict, and deaths have occurred despite antivenom administration in northern Australia. It remains indicated for pain refractory to IV opioids (1 ampoule) and for systemic envenoming with collapse, hypotension, or significant arrhythmia (3 ampoules IV over 20 minutes, repeatable). In cardiac arrest, give all immediately available antivenom (at least 6 ampoules) as a rapid undiluted IV push alongside standard resuscitation and magnesium.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Most stings, once decontaminated, are managed with analgesia and discharge. Any patient with systemic signs or a large-surface-area sting needs cardiorespiratory monitoring in a resuscitation-capable setting.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Vinegar is a decontamination step, not a treatment for pain or systemic symptoms already underway — don't let its application create false reassurance. Antivenom's real-world effectiveness for cardiac arrest is unresolved in the literature; giving it in that scenario is reasonable and recommended, but shouldn't replace aggressive standard resuscitation as the primary intervention.

species.search: irukandji syndrome carukia barnesi carybdeid jellyfish
species.title: Irukandji Syndrome
species.subtitle: Caused by Carukia barnesi and several related small carybdeid jellyfish species. The sting itself is often trivial or unnoticed — the danger is a delayed, severe systemic catecholamine crisis that follows

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: The initial sting is frequently minor — mild local pain, sometimes barely noticed, from a jellyfish that can be nearly invisible in the water. Systemic Irukandji syndrome develops 20-30 minutes later, which is the core diagnostic trap: patients and even early clinicians can dismiss the initial contact as inconsequential before the real syndrome announces itself.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Severe generalized pain (back, limbs, abdomen), profuse sweating, nausea and vomiting, anxiety and a sense of impending doom, hypertension, and tachycardia from a massive catecholamine surge. Severe cases can progress to pulmonary edema, cardiac dysfunction (including stress cardiomyopathy), and rarely fatal intracerebral hemorrhage from the hypertensive crisis. Most patients recover within 24-48 hours with supportive care, but the acute phase is genuinely dangerous.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Vinegar decontamination of the sting site as for box jellyfish. Transport for any patient with delayed severe pain or systemic symptoms after a jellyfish contact in endemic waters — do not be reassured by an initially trivial-seeming sting.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Aggressive analgesia (opioids are often required and may need high doses given the severity of pain). Manage hypertension actively — this is a hypertensive emergency risk, not just a pain syndrome. IV magnesium has trial evidence for symptom control, though a randomized trial found it did not reduce opioid requirement. Monitor for evolving cardiac dysfunction and pulmonary edema; echocardiography is reasonable in more severe presentations.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: No antivenom exists for the carybdeid species causing this syndrome — management is entirely supportive, centered on pain and blood pressure control.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for monitoring given the hypertensive crisis and cardiac risk; most patients recover fully within 24-48 hours, but the acute window needs real cardiorespiratory monitoring capability.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The name-brand danger here is the mismatch between a forgettable sting and a genuinely life-threatening syndrome 20-30 minutes later — treat any patient in endemic waters with delayed severe pain, sweating, and a sense of dread as Irukandji until proven otherwise, even without a clear jellyfish sighting.

species.search: stonefish synanceia
species.title: Stonefish
species.subtitle: Synanceia spp. The most venomous of the spine-bearing fish — venom potency has been compared to cobra venom. Camouflaged on the seafloor; nearly all injuries occur from stepping directly on one

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Venom is released mechanically from dorsal spines under pressure — immediate, severe pain out of proportion to the visible wound, often described as among the most painful stings a person can experience.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Severe local pain and edema, headache, and a distinctively painful cyanotic puncture wound that can progress to necrotic ulceration if untreated. Systemic effects in severe cases can include hypotension and cardiac dysfunction, given cardiotoxic components in the venom.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Hot water immersion (42-45°C, as hot as tolerated without scalding) for 30-90 minutes, or until pain doesn't recur on removal from the water — the venom is heat-labile, making this genuinely effective rather than just comfort care. This is the opposite first-aid principle from jellyfish, which is a common source of confusion in mixed reef environments.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Continue hot water immersion; imaging (X-ray or ultrasound) to check for retained spine fragments, since these are a real source of ongoing pain and infection if missed. Watch for compartment syndrome with significant hand or foot edema — this is a documented complication of severe spine-fish envenomation. Tetanus update and consideration of antibiotics given the puncture mechanism and marine organism exposure.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Stonefish Antivenom (CSL, ovine) exists and is one of the few marine antivenoms with reasonably established use — indicated for severe pain unresponsive to hot water immersion and analgesia, or for systemic envenomation. This is a meaningfully better-supported antivenom situation than box jellyfish or Irukandji.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Most cases resolve with hot water immersion and analgesia alone. Admit for systemic signs, evidence of compartment syndrome, or pain refractory to first aid and antivenom.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Hot water, not vinegar — mixing up the marine decontamination protocols between fish-spine stings and jellyfish stings is a real and consequential error given how different the two mechanisms are. Always image or explore the wound for retained spine material before calling the local injury fully addressed.

species.search: blue-ringed octopus hapalochlaena tetrodotoxin
species.title: Blue-Ringed Octopus
species.subtitle: Hapalochlaena spp. Small, docile, and easily overlooked — bites almost always occur when the animal is picked up or handled, often after being mistaken for an empty shell or curious tide-pool find

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: The bite itself is frequently painless and may go unnoticed at the moment it happens. Symptoms typically begin within minutes to about an hour: perioral numbness and tingling, followed by progressive weakness.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, producing a descending flaccid paralysis: perioral paresthesia, excessive salivation, dysarthria, dysphagia, sweating, dizziness, progressing to muscle weakness, incoordination, and potentially complete flaccid paralysis with respiratory failure. Critically, patients can remain fully conscious and aware throughout complete paralysis — this is a real and psychologically significant feature to communicate and manage for.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure immobilization bandaging is recommended for this bite, unlike jellyfish — wrap firmly from the bite site proximally over the whole limb, since this is a slower-acting neurotoxin where local venom containment genuinely helps, more like a snakebite than a jellyfish sting. Heat does NOT help — tetrodotoxin is heat-stable, so hot water immersion (correct for stonefish) is ineffective here. Be prepared to provide rescue breathing or bag-valve-mask ventilation; this can become necessary quickly and the patient may be unable to signal distress once paralysis sets in.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Intubate for respiratory paralysis or airway compromise from altered consciousness — severe cases typically require assisted ventilation for 2-5 days while the toxin clears. Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia. No antidote exists; this is entirely a supportive-care, buy-time-with-the-ventilator problem.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: None exists. Tetrodotoxin is not an enzyme-based venom in the way most entries on this site are, and there is no product that neutralizes it — full recovery depends on ventilatory support until the toxin is metabolized and cleared.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU admission with ventilator readiness for any patient with paralysis or bulbar signs. Full neurological recovery is the expected outcome with adequate supportive care, even after complete paralysis.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: A patient with complete flaccid paralysis from this bite may be fully conscious and able to hear and understand everything happening around them — communicate accordingly. Don't reach for hot water immersion out of habit from stonefish management; it does nothing for a heat-stable toxin like this one.

species.search: cone snail conus geographer cone geography cone
species.title: Cone Snail
species.subtitle: Conus spp., with the geographer cone (Conus geographus) the most notorious for human fatalities. Injury occurs via a venomous harpoon-like radular tooth, often when a shell is picked up by hand

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Immediate to rapid onset of local pain at the sting site, with numbness and paresthesia that can spread quickly. Severe cases progress to generalized weakness and paralysis within a similar timeframe to blue-ringed octopus envenomation.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom is a complex cocktail of conotoxins (plus tetrodotoxin in some species), producing intense local pain, swelling, numbness, and progressive paralysis that can extend to full respiratory failure in severe cases. Historical fatality rates for the most dangerous species are cited at roughly 25% of significant stings, though modern respiratory support has changed outcomes considerably where available.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure immobilization bandaging, same rationale as blue-ringed octopus — this is a slower-progressing, containable neurotoxin unlike jellyfish venom. Clean the wound with fresh water and watch closely for progressive weakness. Be prepared to provide bag-valve-mask ventilation if paralysis progresses; heat is not an effective decontamination measure for this venom.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial neurologic and respiratory assessment. Intubate proactively for any evidence of progressive respiratory muscle weakness rather than waiting for frank failure — the same buy-time-with-ventilation principle as blue-ringed octopus applies here.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: None exists. Management is entirely supportive, centered on airway and ventilatory support until the venom's effects resolve.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU admission with ventilator readiness for any patient with paralysis or significant systemic symptoms. Full recovery is achievable with adequate supportive care.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: These shells are strikingly beautiful and are the classic reason people pick them up by hand — that's the actual mechanism of injury in the overwhelming majority of cases, not an unprovoked attack. The management principle mirrors blue-ringed octopus closely enough that the two are often taught together: PBI, no heat, ventilate as needed, no antivenom exists for either.

species.search: sea snake enhydrina schistosa beaked sea snake hydrophiidae
species.title: Sea Snakes
species.subtitle: Multiple genera (Hydrophis, Enhydrina, Aipysurus, Laticauda, and others). Marine elapids — closely related to terrestrial cobras and kraits — with potent venom, but bites are uncommon and a large share are "dry" (no venom injected)

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: The bite itself is often painless or minimally painful, and local findings are typically minimal — genuinely easy to underestimate at first contact, similar in spirit to the elapid pattern seen with coral snakes and kraits on land. When envenomation occurs, systemic signs typically develop within 30 minutes to a few hours.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Neurotoxic descending paralysis (ptosis, dysphagia, progressive weakness, respiratory failure in severe cases) combined with a prominent myotoxic component — muscle pain and stiffness, myoglobinuria, and elevated CK, with risk of renal failure from rhabdomyolysis. This myotoxic emphasis is a genuine distinguishing feature from most terrestrial elapids covered elsewhere on this site.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure immobilization bandaging, consistent with the general approach to elapid neurotoxin envenomation — immobilize the limb and transport. Many sea snake encounters (fishing net entanglement is the classic mechanism) result in bites without significant envenomation, but this can't be assumed in the field.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Observation for a reasonable window given how often bites are "dry" — a substantial proportion of sea snake bites do not result in clinically significant envenomation. Serial CK and renal function monitoring given the myotoxic risk, alongside standard neurologic assessment for any signs of progressive weakness.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL Sea Snake Antivenom (Australia, raised primarily against Enhydrina schistosa venom) shows cross-reactivity against venom from multiple other sea snake species and genera. Where sea snake antivenom isn't available, tiger snake antivenom has demonstrated cross-protective activity against sea snake venom in comparative studies and has been used as an alternative.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Observe any confirmed bite for a period sufficient to exclude delayed envenomation, given how often initial presentation is misleadingly benign. Admit for neurologic or myotoxic signs.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: A painless bite with minimal local findings is not reassuring for this group any more than it is for terrestrial elapids — the "dry bite" phenomenon is real and common, but it can't be assumed at first contact, so observation still matters. The myotoxic/rhabdomyolysis angle is worth specifically screening for here, since it's less emphasized in most terrestrial elapid teaching.

species.search: portuguese man o war physalia physalis bluebottle
species.title: Portuguese Man o' War
species.subtitle: Physalia physalis (Atlantic), P. utriculus / "bluebottle" (Pacific). Not a jellyfish at all — a colonial siphonophore — but managed as a marine sting emergency given documented fatalities and a genuine, actively debated first-aid controversy

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Immediate, intense pain on contact with the trailing tentacles, which can extend many meters from the visible floating body — contact doesn't require touching the obvious part of the animal. Pain typically peaks early and fades over 1-3 hours in uncomplicated stings, though systemic reactions can develop over a similar window.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Intense local pain with a whip-like linear sting pattern. Systemic reactions are less common but real: severe muscle cramping, breathing difficulty, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and altered consciousness can indicate a systemic allergic-type reaction requiring prompt medical attention — patients with insect-sting allergies (bees, wasps) may be at elevated risk for a severe reaction here as well. Documented fatalities exist, though they are rare relative to the very high overall sting volume worldwide.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: This is a genuinely unsettled area of first aid, and it's worth knowing both sides rather than treating it as fully resolved. Most current mainstream clinical guidance (dive medicine organizations, several recent case reports) recommends AGAINST vinegar for Physalia specifically — unlike box jellyfish — and instead favors seawater or hot-water rinsing, on the basis that vinegar may trigger further nematocyst discharge for this genus. However, a 2017 peer-reviewed study directly testing this question found vinegar effective and safe for Physalia, and found that seawater rinsing actually spread stinging cells over more area and made stings worse in their model — directly contradicting the historical seawater recommendation. Given genuinely conflicting evidence, follow current regional/institutional protocol rather than assuming either approach is settled; whichever fluid is used, avoid rubbing the area, fresh water, alcohol, and ammonia, which are more consistently identified as harmful across studies. After decontamination, 45°C hot water immersion for about 45 minutes has support for inactivating already-injected venom and reducing pain.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Continue pain control with hot water immersion; regional nerve blocks (case reports describe erector spinae plane blocks) have been used for severe, extensive stings refractory to standard analgesia. Monitor for and treat systemic allergic-type reactions per standard anaphylaxis management if they develop — antihistamines and corticosteroids for milder systemic symptoms, escalating per usual allergic-reaction protocols for severe presentations.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: None exists. The only jellyfish/cnidarian antivenom in existence worldwide is the CSL box jellyfish product, which does not cover Physalia — management here is entirely decontamination and supportive/symptomatic care.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Most stings resolve with first aid and analgesia alone. Any patient with systemic symptoms — especially breathing difficulty, chest pain, or a sting covering a large body surface area — needs prompt medical evaluation and monitoring.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't reflexively apply the box jellyfish vinegar protocol here without knowing this is a live, unresolved debate specific to Physalia — this is exactly the kind of cross-species first-aid mix-up this page is trying to prevent elsewhere (see stonefish vs. jellyfish, blue-ringed octopus vs. stonefish). Detached tentacles washed up on the beach can still sting effectively even after the animal has died — treat beached specimens as live hazards.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Stingray
items.html: — venom itself is not typically life-threatening; the danger from this animal is almost entirely mechanical trauma from the barb, which can rarely be fatal with deep penetrating chest or abdominal injury (treat that scenario as trauma, not envenomation). Care: hot water immersion for pain (venom is heat-labile, same principle as stonefish), wound exploration and imaging for retained barb fragments, tetanus update.

items.name: Sea Urchin
items.html: — spine puncture wounds cause pain and local irritation; retained spine fragments are the main real complication, not the mild venom itself. Care: spine removal (may require imaging to locate fragments), hot water immersion for pain, watch for delayed granuloma formation around retained fragments.

regions.label: Middle East
regions.lede: Three species drive the overwhelming majority of medically significant envenomation in this region. All have narrow, geography-specific antivenom requirements — a product that works for one population of the same species elsewhere is not a safe assumption here.

species.search: saw-scaled viper echis coloratus echis carinatus arabian carpet viper
species.title: Saw-Scaled Viper
species.subtitle: Echis coloratus (Arabian/Levant saw-scaled viper — Israel, Jordan, Arabian Peninsula) and E. carinatus (Persian Gulf, Iran, further east). Second most common cause of snake envenomation in Israel; one of "the Big Four" venomous snakes across the broader Middle East/South Asia range

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling within minutes of the bite. Hemostatic failure follows, though timeline and severity vary meaningfully between species/populations — E. coloratus in Israel is associated with lower mortality (rare, isolated fatalities from renal failure) than E. carinatus further east, where regional mortality estimates run higher.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Local swelling plus venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy. Roughly one-third of victims bleed or develop anemia. Severe outcomes (hemorrhage, acute kidney injury) are the exception rather than the rule with E. coloratus specifically, but should still be anticipated and screened for in every case.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize the limb, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Baseline and serial coagulation studies, renal function, and urinalysis (proteinuria is a treatment-threshold marker, see below). A bedside whole blood clotting test is a reasonable adjunct where formal coags are slow to return.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: A regional monovalent equine IgG antivenom is used for E. coloratus envenomation, dosed by symptoms rather than a fixed protocol: an initial 20 mL IV dose for systemic involvement, with repeat 10 mL doses for relapse. In outcome data, 49% of patients showed no systemic symptoms and received no antivenom at all; of those treated, 63% resolved with a single 20 mL dose. A published decision model favors treating when bleeding risk is elevated — specifically with proteinuria, BUN >7 mmol/L, platelet count <100,000/µL, or hemoglobin <13 g/dL — rather than treating every confirmed bite empirically.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit any suspected bite for coagulation monitoring regardless of initial appearance. Antivenom decision follows the symptom/lab-based threshold above rather than universal empiric dosing.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Echis antivenoms have documented narrow cross-reactivity — a product developed against one regional population (e.g., West African E. ocellatus, or Indian E. carinatus) is not reliably interchangeable with what's needed here, and mismatched antivenom has caused real treatment failures. Confirm the specific regional product your facility stocks. Serum sickness occurs in a notable share of antivenom-treated patients (reported as high as 44% in one series) — this is a real cost of treatment that factors into the symptom-triggered approach rather than treating everyone empirically.

species.search: deathstalker scorpion leiurus quinquestriatus palestine yellow scorpion omdurman scorpion israeli desert scorpion naqab desert scorpion
species.title: Deathstalker Scorpion
species.subtitle: Leiurus quinquestriatus. Also called: Palestine yellow scorpion, Omdurman scorpion, Israeli desert scorpion, Naqab desert scorpion. Rarely fatal in healthy adults — dangerous mainly to children, the elderly, and those with cardiac disease

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Sting pain is immediate and severe. In vulnerable patients — overwhelmingly children — systemic signs can progress over hours to a catecholamine-driven autonomic storm.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom neurotoxins act on sodium and potassium channels, driving a massive catecholamine surge. In severe pediatric envenomation this produces hypertension, tachycardia, cardiogenic shock, and pulmonary edema, alongside CNS findings — lethargy, confusion, agitation, and reduced consciousness. A high rate of pancreatitis has been reported in Israeli case series following envenomation. Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps are common even in milder cases. Healthy adults typically experience severe local pain without progressing to this systemic picture.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Analgesia and urgent transport, with a markedly lower threshold for urgency in pediatric, elderly, or cardiac-history patients — this is where the rare fatalities occur.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Local infiltration (1% lidocaine, digital block for a digit sting) is an effective, underused option for pain control. For hypertension and the catecholamine-driven cardiovascular picture, alpha-blockade (prazosin) or hydralazine have shown benefit in case series and small trials; beta-blockers, cardiac glycosides, and high-dose corticosteroids are not recommended. Mechanical ventilation and full ICU support for pulmonary edema or respiratory failure in severe pediatric cases.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Multiple regional products exist — the National Antivenom and Vaccine Production Center (Riyadh, Saudi Arabia), Sanofi Pasteur (France), and Twyford (Germany) all manufacture Leiurus-directed antivenom. None are FDA-approved in the US; access there is investigational-only (the US Armed Forces and the Florida Antivenin Bank hold IND applications for military/emergency use). Exact dosing for non-Centruroides scorpion antivenoms remains poorly established — treatment is guided by clinical severity and response rather than a fixed protocol, unlike the well-defined Anascorp dosing for North American Centruroides.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Any pediatric patient with systemic signs needs ICU-capable care given the cardiogenic and CNS risk. Healthy adults with isolated severe local pain can typically be managed with analgesia and observation.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The core danger here is age-dependent, not dose-dependent in the way many envenomations are — a sting that's "just very painful" in an adult can be genuinely life-threatening in a child from the same scorpion. Don't extrapolate reassurance from an adult presentation to a pediatric one. Confirm which regional antivenom product (if any) is actually accessible before it's needed — availability varies significantly by country.

species.search: levant viper blunt-nosed viper macrovipera lebetina
species.title: Levant Viper
species.subtitle: Macrovipera lebetina. Also called: blunt-nosed viper. One of the largest and most dangerous vipers across its range, spanning the Levant, parts of the Arabian Peninsula, Cyprus, and into Central Asia

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Significant local pain and swelling develop rapidly given the species' large size and substantial venom yield; systemic coagulopathy follows over the subsequent hours.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Severe local tissue effects — swelling, blistering, and necrosis risk — combined with venom-induced consumption coagulopathy and systemic hemorrhage. Bites from this species are considered among the most medically significant viper envenomations in its range given the combination of large body size, substantial venom yield, and potent hemotoxic activity.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial coagulation studies and limb assessment as for other major regional vipers. Aggressive wound care given real necrosis risk from the substantial local tissue destruction this species can cause.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Regional coverage is genuinely fragmented across this species' wide range. The Razi Vaccine and Serum Research Institute (Iran) produces a pentavalent/hexavalent product specifically covering M. lebetina obtusa alongside several other regional vipers. Egyptian VACSERA polyvalent antivenom has also demonstrated cross-neutralization against Macrovipera lebetina species in laboratory studies. Confirm which specific regional product is stocked — this is not a species with one simple continent-wide antivenom answer.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation monitoring and aggressive wound surveillance given the necrosis risk from this species' substantial local tissue destruction potential.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't underestimate this species relative to the smaller, more frequently discussed saw-scaled viper on this page — Levant viper bites carry real severity from sheer venom volume alone, and antivenom sourcing needs to be confirmed for the specific country/region rather than assumed.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Camel Spider
items.html: (Solifugae — not a true spider) — large, fast-moving, and alarming in appearance with powerful jaws that can cause a mechanically painful bite, but not venomous at all. Care: clean the wound, standard laceration/puncture care; no antivenom exists because none is needed.

items.name: Field/Common Scorpions
items.html: (Buthus spp. and similar, excluding deathstalker) — painful sting, local swelling; not typically dangerous to healthy adults. Care: ice, analgesia, reassurance; treat pediatric or elderly patients with the same caution as any scorpion sting until deathstalker exposure is excluded.

regions.label: North America
regions.lede: Pit vipers cause the overwhelming majority of US snakebite, but this page also covers the one species where local swelling actively misleads (Mojave rattlesnake) and the two arthropods where antivenom decisions carry real tradeoffs of their own (black widow, bark scorpion).

species.search: pit viper crotalinae rattlesnake copperhead cottonmouth rattler diamondback sidewinder highland moccasin chunk head water moccasin gapper crofab anavip
species.title: Pit Vipers (Rattlesnake, Copperhead, Cottonmouth)
species.subtitle: Crotalinae — ~98% of US venomous snakebites. Also called: rattler, diamondback, sidewinder (rattlesnake) · highland moccasin, chunk head (copperhead) · water moccasin, gapper (cottonmouth)

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Pain and local swelling begin within minutes. Copperhead and cottonmouth bites are dominated by local tissue effects; rattlesnake bites more often produce early, late, and recurrent coagulopathy layered on top of local injury. Coagulopathy can lag the local exam by hours and can recur after initial control.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Progressive edema, ecchymosis, and hemorrhagic bullae at the bite site. Hematologic effects: thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, elevated PT/PTT. Systemic signs when significant: hypotension, perioral or extremity paresthesias, metallic or rubbery taste, nausea.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Remove rings, watches, and constricting clothing before swelling progresses. Immobilize the extremity at heart level. Mark and time the leading edge of swelling/erythema for serial comparison. Do not use tourniquets, ice, incision, suction, or electrical shock — none are proven and several cause harm. Avoid NSAIDs given bleeding risk. Rapid transport; no field antivenom.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Baseline CBC, platelets, PT/PTT, fibrinogen. Re-mark leading edge every 15–30 minutes until progression stops. True compartment syndrome from crotalid envenomation is rare — most tense swelling is subcutaneous, not compartmental; prophylactic fasciotomy is not recommended and compartment pressure measurement should be reserved for exam findings inconsistent with venom effect alone.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Two FDA-approved products, both effective for all three US pit viper genera. CroFab (FabAV): initial dose 4–6 vials (4 vials for isolated copperhead bites), often needs scheduled maintenance dosing (2 vials q6h × 3 doses after initial control) to prevent recurrence. Anavip (Fab2AV): fixed initial dose of 10 vials regardless of age, longer half-life associated with lower rates of late/recurrent coagulopathy, no standard maintenance dose but more patients need repeat initial-control dosing (registry data: median 18 vials Anavip vs 10 vials CroFab to reach control). Reassess q1h against exam and labs; redose either product until initial control achieved — arrest of local progression, improving systemic signs, correcting coagulopathy.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Observe a minimum of 18–24 hours after initial control regardless of antivenom used. Recheck coagulation labs 6–12 hours after control, again prior to discharge, and twice after discharge given recurrence risk — this applies to both products but especially CroFab.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: No prehospital intervention has ever been proven to change outcome — the job in the field is removing constricting items and getting the patient to antivenom, nothing else. Watch for alpha-gal (galactose-α-1,3-galactose) sensitization causing anaphylactoid reactions to CroFab, which is sheep-derived — regionally more relevant in the southeastern US where tick-associated alpha-gal allergy is common. Recurrent coagulopathy after apparent control is a real phenomenon, not a monitoring failure — this is why the discharge lab schedule exists.

species.search: coral snake elapidae micrurus candy stick candy snake nacsa
species.title: Coral Snake
species.subtitle: Micrurus fulvius (Eastern), M. tener (Texas). Also called: candy stick, candy snake. Delayed neurotoxicity — distinct course from pit vipers

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Deceptive. Local findings at the bite are often minimal or absent — no significant pain or swelling like a pit viper bite. Neurologic signs can be delayed several hours before appearing, and once they start, progression can be rapid and does not reliably reverse with antivenom once established.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Bulbar findings first: ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia. Progresses to generalized skeletal muscle weakness and paralysis, then respiratory failure if untreated. The mismatch between an unimpressive bite site and the eventual severity is the core danger.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Same general principles as pit viper — immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. The critical field task is not under-triaging a bite just because it looks unremarkable.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Extended observation is mandatory even in asymptomatic patients, given delayed onset — historically 24 hours. Frequent neurologic and respiratory checks (cranial nerves, vital capacity/NIF if any bulbar signs appear). Have airway equipment ready; these patients can progress to needing prolonged ventilator support.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: North American Coral Snake Antivenin (NACSA, Wyeth/Pfizer) is the only FDA-approved product and production stopped in 2003. Remaining stock has run on serial FDA expiration-date extensions of a single lot (CL6814) for years; check current lot status with poison control (1-800-222-1222) since availability is not guaranteed and changes. Dose 3–5 vials in adults, decreased in small children per response. There is no other FDA-approved alternative in the US; Mexican Coralmyn (Bioclon) has been used via special arrangement in some shortage situations. Historic practice was empiric treatment of any suspected bite given irreversible neurotoxicity risk; more recent data suggest a symptom-triggered approach doesn't worsen outcomes and avoids adverse events from treating asymptomatic patients — but this is a genuine access-driven tradeoff, not just a clinical preference, given how scarce the product is.

fields.label: Disposition
