fields.html: Minimum 12–24 hour observation even if asymptomatic at presentation, given delayed onset. Any neurologic sign warrants ICU-level monitoring.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: "Red touch yellow, kill a fellow; red touch black, venom lack" distinguishes coral snake from mimics like the scarlet kingsnake in the US — this rhyme does not reliably apply outside North America and should never be used to clear a bite in another region. Minimal local findings are not reassurance — they are the expected presentation. Antivenom scarcity is a real operational constraint here, not a hypothetical; know your hospital's and region's current supply before you need it.

species.search: black widow latrodectus latrodectism hourglass spider shoe button spider lyovac
species.title: Black Widow
species.subtitle: Latrodectus mactans and related spp. Also called: hourglass spider, shoe button spider. Syndrome: latrodectism

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Sharp pinprick pain at the bite site, then local cramping that spreads over 15 minutes to a few hours. Untreated, the syndrome typically runs 1–3 days.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Severe muscle cramping and rigidity — abdominal wall can become boardlike and mimic a surgical abdomen, but without true peritoneal tenderness. Autonomic findings: diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension. Bite site itself is often unremarkable, so the exam and history carry more weight than the wound.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Supportive — analgesia as tolerated, transport. No field-specific antidote or intervention beyond comfort measures.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Opioids and benzodiazepines are the mainstay for pain and rigidity control, though often only partially effective. Calcium gluconate has been used historically for muscle cramping but evidence is weak and it is not a substitute for antivenom in severe cases.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Merck's Lyovac Antivenin (Latrodectus mactans) — whole equine IgG — remains the product available in North America, though manufacturer low-inventory periods occur and current stock should be confirmed with poison control. Reserved for severe or refractory envenomation: seizures, hypertensive crisis, respiratory compromise, or intractable pain unresponsive to opioids and benzodiazepines. Dose: 1 vial diluted in 50 mL NS, IV over 15–30 minutes. Skin or conjunctival sensitivity testing is required first given real anaphylaxis risk (reported up to ~5%); history of asthma or atopy is a relative contraindication. Fear of this reaction is the main reason antivenom is underused in the US relative to how effective it is.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Most cases are managed with supportive care and observation without antivenom. Admit for antivenom administration or refractory symptoms.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Consider latrodectism in unexplained abdominal rigidity without true peritoneal signs, especially with autonomic findings and a plausible exposure — garages, woodpiles, outdoor storage. The bite site will often not help you; the history and autonomic picture will. Antivenom underuse in US practice reflects genuine reluctance around the anaphylaxis rate, not a lack of efficacy — know the skin-test protocol before you need it.

species.search: centruroides bark scorpion arizona sculptured scorpion anascorp
species.title: Bark Scorpion
species.subtitle: Centruroides sculpturatus. Clinically significant scorpion in the US, concentrated in the Southwest (Arizona and neighboring states)

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Pain at the sting site is immediate and often out of proportion to visible findings — there's usually no significant local lesion. Systemic neurotoxic signs, when they occur, can develop within 30 minutes to a few hours, especially in young children.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Graded severity. Grade I–II: local pain and paresthesias only. Grade III–IV: either cranial nerve dysfunction (roving/abnormal eye movements, blurred vision, slurred speech, dysphagia) or somatic skeletal neuromuscular dysfunction (jerking, restlessness) — or both. The somatic findings in kids can look like seizure activity but are not epileptic.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Analgesia and transport, with lower threshold for urgency in pediatric patients or anyone with early cranial nerve or neuromuscular signs.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Grade the envenomation on cranial nerve and somatic findings to decide on antivenom. Prior to antivenom availability, severe cases were managed with benzodiazepines, sedation, and occasionally intubation for supportive control — that approach is now reserved for cases where antivenom is unavailable or as an adjunct.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Anascorp (equine F(ab')2) — initial dose is a fixed 3 vials IV over 10 minutes regardless of age or weight, for any patient with Grade III–IV signs. Additional 1-vial doses may be given every 30–60 minutes based on symptom resolution. Mean time to symptom resolution after treatment is roughly 1.4 hours. Distribution is exclusive through AnovoRx rather than standard pharmacy wholesale — a stocking/logistics point worth knowing before a shortage-of-time situation, not during one.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Patients typically can be discharged home once symptoms resolve after antivenom, often within a few hours of treatment.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The "tap test" — light tapping over the sting site reproducing severe pain with no visible lesion — is a useful bedside clue that distinguishes this from other bites/stings. There's active debate over whether the fixed 3-vial initial dose is necessary versus a 1-vial-then-reassess strategy for Grade III–IV envenomation; this is evolving practice, not settled. Pediatric patients remain the population most likely to progress to severe neurotoxicity.

species.search: mojave rattlesnake crotalus scutulatus mojave green mojave toxin
species.title: Mojave Rattlesnake
species.subtitle: Crotalus scutulatus. Also called: Mojave green (though color varies — green, brown, yellow, gray). The pit viper that breaks the "pit vipers are hemotoxic" rule taught for every other species on this page

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling on bite, similar to other pit vipers initially — but this species carries a real risk of a very different second act, depending on which venom phenotype delivered the bite.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: This species has at least two distinct venom phenotypes, and telling them apart matters clinically. Type A venom is dominated by Mojave toxin (MTX), a potent presynaptic β-neurotoxin with little hemorrhagic activity — bites can progress to weakness, ptosis, and respiratory compromise with deceptively unimpressive local swelling, genuinely unusual for a North American pit viper. Type B venom lacks MTX and instead is rich in hemorrhagic metalloproteinases — a more typical crotalid picture of significant local tissue damage and coagulopathy. Mixed Type A+B individuals also exist, and some populations additionally carry a distinct myotoxin (Type M). Geography offers only a rough guide: Type A predominates in California, southern Nevada, southwest Utah, and parts of Arizona/New Mexico/Texas, while Type B is concentrated in central Arizona — but populations overlap and mix, so the venom type of any individual snake can't be assumed from location alone.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard pit viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Given the neurotoxic risk, monitor for early bulbar or respiratory signs even if local swelling looks unimpressive — don't let a mild-looking bite site delay transport.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Assess for both pictures — coagulation studies as for any pit viper bite, AND close neurologic/respiratory monitoring given the real possibility of a Type A envenomation. A bite with minimal local swelling but early neurologic complaints should raise this species specifically, especially in its range.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CroFab and Anavip are both derived from venom pools that include Mojave rattlesnake venom and are considered effective against this species, including the Type A neurotoxic component — this is not a species requiring a separate antivenom, unlike several other regional-specificity cases on this site. Standard pit viper dosing and initial-control principles apply.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Extend the standard pit-viper observation window with a lower threshold for prolonged neurologic monitoring, given that significant neurotoxicity can develop despite modest local findings.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: This is the one North American pit viper where "mild local swelling" is not reassuring on its own — a Type A envenomation can be doing its real damage neurologically while the bite site looks unremarkable. Don't apply the general crotalid teaching point (local findings track severity) uncritically to a confirmed or suspected Mojave rattlesnake bite.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: These North American species cause real pain/reaction but are not typically life-threatening and do not require antivenom or critical-care level intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Brown Recluse
items.html: (fiddleback, violin spider) — most bites self-limited; minority progress to local necrotic lesion over days. Care: conservative wound care, no early debridement; rare pediatric systemic hemolysis is the exception — admit if it occurs.

items.name: Hymenoptera
items.html: (bee/wasp/hornet/fire ant) — local pain and, with fire ants, a sterile pustule. Care: ice, analgesia; systemic/allergic reaction routes to Anaphylaxis, not this page.

items.name: Gila Monster
items.html: — tenacious chewing bite, painful, occasional hypotension/anaphylactoid reaction; no US deaths reported in 70+ years. Care: wound irrigation, remove retained teeth, supportive care; observe ~6h.

items.name: Puss Caterpillar
items.html: (asp, tree asp) — severe burning contact pain from hidden spines, resolves within hours. Care: tape-strip spine removal (don't scrape), ice, antihistamines.

items.name: Velvet Ant
items.html: ("cow killer") — dramatic pain, minimal actual severity. Care: reassurance, ice, analgesia.

regions.label: SE Asia & Oceania
regions.lede: Australian elapids carry some of the most potent venoms in the world by laboratory measures, but clinical importance tracks bite frequency and human contact more than raw toxicity — the snake that bites people most often, not the one with the scariest LD50, drives regional mortality. Four distinct Australian elapid genera are covered here since their management differs enough to matter clinically.

species.search: coastal taipan oxyuranus scutellatus papuan taipan inland taipan
species.title: Coastal Taipan
species.subtitle: Oxyuranus scutellatus. Widely cited as having one of the most toxic venoms of any land snake by laboratory LD50. The related inland taipan (O. microlepidotus) is even more toxic per bite but lives in remote desert with almost no human contact — coastal taipan is the one that actually bites people

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: The majority of significant bites develop systemic envenoming — this is not a species where "wait and see" is a reasonable default. Clinical or laboratory evidence of envenoming is usually apparent within 2 hours, though effective pressure immobilization can delay this.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Combines neurotoxicity, myotoxicity, venom-induced consumption coagulopathy, acute kidney injury, and thrombocytopenia — a genuinely multi-system envenomation rather than one dominant mechanism. In a large case series, roughly two-thirds of systemically envenomed patients had neurotoxicity and about 40% had complete or partial VICC.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure bandage with immobilization (PBI) is the standard Australian first-aid approach for all elapid bites — firm elastic bandage over the bite site, then the entire limb, plus a rigid splint, with the whole patient kept still. This is a materially different approach from North American snakebite first aid (no tourniquet or bandaging there) — know which region's protocol applies.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Leave the PBI in place until antivenom and resuscitation facilities are ready — removal can precipitate rapid systemic deterioration as sequestered venom releases. The Snake Venom Detection Kit (SVDK) can help select which monovalent antivenom to use when more than one species is possible, but it is not a diagnostic test for envenoming itself and produces both false positives and negatives.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL monovalent Taipan Antivenom (equine). One vial has been shown to bind all measurable venom in confirmed bites, and early antivenom administration is associated with better outcomes — this is a species where speed matters more than dose escalation. Typical dosing is 1 vial diluted in saline, IV over 20–30 minutes (undiluted rapid push if hemodynamically unstable or in arrest); total doses in case series have ranged 1–9 vials depending on severity. CSL polyvalent antivenom is an alternative when species identification is uncertain, at the cost of higher volume and anaphylaxis risk.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit any patient with confirmed or strongly suspected envenoming for coagulation, renal, and neurologic monitoring. Ventilator support may be needed for significant neurotoxicity.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't confuse "most toxic venom in the world" (inland taipan, by lab measures) with "most clinically important" — coastal taipan and eastern brown snake account for the overwhelming majority of actual severe Australian envenomations because they're the ones people encounter. Taipan and brown snake antivenoms are species-specific with little cross-protection — the right monovalent product matters.

species.search: eastern brown snake pseudonaja textilis
species.title: Eastern Brown Snake
species.subtitle: Pseudonaja textilis. The single most medically important snake in Australia by case volume — widespread, common near farmland and urban fringes, and responsible for the majority of Australian snakebite deaths despite venom that is less exotic-sounding than taipan's

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: A distinctive and dangerous feature: sudden collapse can occur very early after the bite, sometimes before any other envenoming signs are apparent — this is thought to reflect a rapid, direct cardiovascular effect distinct from the coagulopathy that develops afterward.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Early collapse and, in about 5% of envenomed patients, frank cardiac arrest — a genuine outlier among snakebites for how early cardiovascular collapse can occur. Venom-induced consumption coagulopathy follows in most systemically envenomed patients, presenting as bleeding gums or IV-site oozing, rarely progressing to intracerebral or intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Thrombotic microangiopathy (thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, acute renal failure) occurs in roughly 10% of envenomings. Significant neurotoxicity is uncommon despite a neurotoxin being present in the venom — mild diplopia or ptosis can occur but frank paralysis is rare, unlike taipan or tiger snake.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Same PBI approach as other Australian elapids — firm bandage over the bite site, then the whole limb, plus splinting and immobilization of the entire patient.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Watch specifically for early collapse and be ready to manage cardiac arrest even before coagulopathy has had time to develop — this can be the first sign of envenoming, not a late complication. If arrest occurs, undiluted antivenom should be given as a rapid IV push alongside standard resuscitation, rather than the slower diluted-infusion approach used for stable patients.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL monovalent Brown Snake Antivenom, indicated for systemic symptoms, collapse, cardiac arrest, or laboratory evidence of complete or partial VICC, within roughly 12 hours of the bite. Dosing has genuine ongoing controversy in the Australian toxinology literature — some data support higher doses than historically used, while also flagging that unnecessarily high doses may not add benefit; this is an area of active study rather than a settled protocol.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation monitoring and cardiovascular observation given the early-collapse risk. Watch for evolving thrombotic microangiopathy independent of the coagulopathy picture.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't be reassured by an early, otherwise well-appearing patient — the sudden collapse phenomenon means brown snake envenoming can announce itself with cardiac arrest before any bleeding sign has developed. This is the Australian species where "looks fine right now" carries the least reassurance.

species.search: tiger snake notechis scutatus notechis ater
species.title: Tiger Snake
species.subtitle: Notechis scutatus (mainland tiger snake) and N. ater (black tiger snake). The most important venomous snake in Tasmania and among the most frequent causes of envenoming in Victoria

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: A genuinely multi-system envenomation, similar in breadth to taipan. In a large prospective series, venom-induced consumption coagulopathy was near-universal (53 of 56 confirmed cases), with systemic symptoms, myotoxicity, and neurotoxicity all occurring at meaningful rates in the same population.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: VICC, systemic symptoms, myotoxicity (with substantial creatine kinase elevation and rhabdomyolysis risk), and neurotoxicity. The principal neurotoxin, notexin, acts presynaptically and physically destroys synaptic terminals and vesicles — this is a structural injury, not a reversible receptor blockade, which matters directly for treatment (see below). Post-bite collapse can occur and its significance is easily under-recognized.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure bandage with immobilization (PBI), same as other Australian elapids.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Watch for rhabdomyolysis-driven renal injury given the myotoxic component — this is more prominent here than in brown snake envenoming. Because notexin destroys presynaptic terminals rather than blocking them reversibly, neostigmine will not restore acetylcholine release the way it might for a purely postsynaptic block — if used at all, it should be paired with atropine to prevent bradycardia, but don't expect it to meaningfully reverse established paralysis.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL monovalent Tiger Snake Antivenom. One vial has been shown sufficient to bind all circulating venom in confirmed bites, matching the dose originally recommended when the product was first released. Notably, case data show clinical benefit from antivenom even when given after a substantial delay (one case report documents recovery after a 48-hour delay) — don't withhold treatment on the assumption that "too much time has passed."

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation, renal, and neurologic monitoring given the multi-system involvement. CK trend matters as much as coagulation labs here.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't treat a period of apparent stability after the bite as reassurance — post-bite collapse is a recognized and sometimes under-appreciated feature. The structural (not receptor-blocking) nature of notexin's neurotoxicity is the key mechanistic reason neostigmine underperforms here relative to death adder, where postsynaptic blockade is more prominent.

species.search: death adder acanthophis antarcticus
species.regionTag: Australia, Papua New Guinea, eastern Indonesia
species.title: Death Adder
species.subtitle: Acanthophis antarcticus and related species. An ambush predator, unlike the actively foraging brown and tiger snakes — bites often happen when the snake is stepped on or disturbed rather than encountered moving

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Neurotoxicity develops in roughly half of definite bites in case series, typically presenting over hours. This is the one Australian elapid where a genuinely important lab caveat applies (see below).

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Predominantly neurotoxic: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar weakness, and intercostal muscle weakness in a descending pattern similar in character to krait or coral snake. Critically, death adder venom is NOT significantly coagulopathic — this breaks the general Australian-elapid rule that a normal coagulation screen argues against significant envenoming. A normal 20WBCT or coag panel does not clear a death adder bite the way it would for brown, tiger, or taipan.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: PBI as for other Australian elapid bites. Given the ambush-predator bite mechanism, consider this diagnosis even without a clear "snake encounter" history — a bite from stepping near or on a motionless snake fits this species' pattern.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Do not rely on coagulation studies to rule this out. One vial of antivenom is effective at binding circulating venom, but — much like krait and black mamba — this does not reliably reverse neurotoxicity that has already developed; average time to resolution of neurotoxicity is about a day regardless of treatment. Some case reports describe neostigmine response, reflecting a real postsynaptic component to this venom's neurotoxicity (in contrast to tiger snake's more structural, presynaptic damage) — a trial is reasonable but should never substitute for airway readiness.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL monovalent Death Adder Antivenom, raised against Acanthophis antarcticus and effective across the death adder species found in Australia and Papua New Guinea.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for neurologic and respiratory monitoring regardless of coagulation results. Ventilator readiness for any bulbar or respiratory signs.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The single most important teaching point for this species: normal clotting studies do not rule out significant death adder envenoming, unlike every other major Australian elapid on this page. Base the treatment decision on the clinical neurologic exam, not the coagulation panel.

species.search: sydney funnel-web spider atrax robustus hadronyche
species.title: Sydney Funnel-Web Spider
species.subtitle: Atrax robustus and related genus Hadronyche. The only spider in the world managed with the same pressure-immobilization first aid as a venomous snakebite — a genuine exception among spider envenomations

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Severe systemic envenoming develops fast — median onset around 28 minutes, usually within 2 hours, and death can occur within about 15 minutes in small children if untreated. Only male spiders cause serious envenomation; the toxin (δ-hexatoxin) has no equivalent effect in other mammals, which is part of why this genus is so specifically dangerous to humans.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: A two-phase picture. Phase 1: local pain (fang marks present, but notably little local swelling or redness), then perioral paresthesias and fasciculations prominent in the tongue, face, and intercostal muscles, progressing to autonomic storm — sweating, salivation, lacrimation, piloerection, hypertension, tachycardia — with airway compromise possible from muscle spasm and, in some cases, pulmonary edema causing death in this phase. Phase 2: adrenergic/cholinergic effects subside, followed by a deceptively calm period, then refractory hypotension, apnea, and cardiac arrest can follow if untreated. Children may present atypically with sudden inconsolable crying, salivation, vomiting, or collapse rather than the adult symptom pattern.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Pressure immobilization bandage — identical technique to snakebite. This is one of the few spider bites where PBI is indicated; do not extrapolate this to other spiders (see the non-critical notice below for the exception this creates with redback bites). Funnel-web venom is unusual in that local tissue inactivation of venom occurs with sustained pressure, so effective PBI genuinely buys time — laboratory data suggest up to 2 mg of venom can be inactivated over 24 hours of maintained pressure, well above what a bite typically delivers.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Do not remove the PBI until antivenom and resuscitation capability are ready — removal can precipitate rapid symptom onset. Observe for at least 4–6 hours post-envenomation and at least 2 hours after bandage removal before ruling out significant envenoming; only 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 bites become seriously ill, so mild presentations are genuinely common and don't all need antivenom. Aggressive supportive care (analgesia, blood pressure control, non-invasive or invasive ventilation) may be needed while antivenom is sourced or the patient remains critical.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: CSL Funnel-Web Spider Antivenom (rabbit-derived IgG), introduced in 1981 — no confirmed deaths have occurred since its introduction when appropriately administered, a genuinely dramatic before/after given 13+ known deaths in the pre-antivenom era. Effective against the broader funnel-web group beyond just Atrax robustus, and also used for mouse spider (Missulena spp.) envenomation. Initial dose 2 ampoules IV for systemic signs (4 ampoules for severe signs like ARDS or altered mental status); repeat 2 ampoules at 15 minutes if incompletely reversed; cardiac arrest warrants at least 4 ampoules as a rapid undiluted IV push alongside resuscitation. Severe allergic reaction occurs in roughly 1.3% of recipients.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU-level observation for any patient with systemic signs. Even confirmed severe envenoming carries a good prognosis with timely antivenom and supportive care.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Any large black spider bite in NSW or southern Queensland should be treated as a possible funnel-web until proven otherwise, given how much this changes the first-aid approach (PBI, unlike almost every other spider bite). Absent local swelling with severe local pain is a notable feature — don't expect visible inflammation to match the severity of the pain.

species.search: king cobra ophiophagus hannah
species.regionTag: SE Asia, S. China, parts of India
species.title: King Cobra
species.subtitle: Ophiophagus hannah. The world's longest venomous snake. Venom is only moderately toxic drop-for-drop compared to many smaller elapids, but the volume delivered per bite is enormous — up to 400–600 mg — which is what makes bites so dangerous

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Can progress to fatality within 30 minutes in severe cases. This snake tends to "bite and hold," delivering more venom the longer contact is maintained — a distinct behavioral risk factor compared to snakes that strike and release.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Local findings can include dusky discoloration, swelling, and pain, with severe cases extending to proximal swelling, necrosis, and tissue sloughing that may require amputation. Systemically: blurred vision, vertigo, drowsiness, and progressive descending paralysis, potentially reaching cardiovascular collapse and respiratory failure. Reported mortality in some case series runs as high as 50–60% without prompt treatment — genuinely higher than most other elapid bites, reflecting the combination of high venom volume and rarity of clinical experience treating it.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Bites are rare in the wild (the species avoids humans and mostly preys on other snakes) but occur disproportionately among reptile handlers, zookeepers, and collectors — most documented cases are occupational or captive-animal exposures rather than wild encounters. Rapid transport is critical given the fast progression.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Airway support and ventilation are frequently required — case reports describe rapid intubation for bulbar and respiratory paralysis. If treating a king cobra bite outside its native range (e.g., an exotic pet or zoo exposure), contact the regional poison control center or a zoo with exotic antivenom access immediately; sourcing the correct product is a genuine logistical race against time in these cases.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: The Thai Red Cross Society (Queen Saovabha Memorial Institute, Bangkok) produces the only species-specific King Cobra monovalent antivenom in the world, raised against Thai-origin venom. A Thai Neuro-Polyvalent antivenom (covering king cobra, monocled cobra, banded krait, and Malayan krait) is a reasonable alternative when the monospecific product isn't available, though at generally lower potency against king cobra specifically. Documented case reports show recovery with doses ranging widely — from single digits up to 33 vials — reflecting real variability in venom load and presentation severity; expect to titrate against clinical response rather than anchor to one number. Antivenom raised against Thai-origin venom shows reduced effectiveness against king cobra populations from other geographic regions (Indonesia, China) given documented venom composition differences — another entry in this page's recurring geographic-variation theme.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU admission with ventilator readiness for any confirmed bite. Recovery with adequate, timely antivenom and supportive care — including prolonged ventilation where needed — is achievable even in severe cases, per multiple published full-recovery case reports.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Local necrosis can be significant enough to require surgical debridement or amputation — this isn't a purely neurotoxic bite the way krait is; treat the wound as seriously as the airway. Given how rare confirmed bites are worldwide, involving a toxinologist or exotic-animal-experienced poison center early is genuinely valuable rather than optional.

species.search: malayan pit viper calloselasma rhodostoma
species.title: Malayan Pit Viper
species.subtitle: Calloselasma rhodostoma. The species responsible for the largest share of snakebite poisoning cases in Thailand (roughly 38% in national data) — bad-tempered, quick to strike, and known for staying in place at the bite scene rather than fleeing

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling develop rapidly at the bite site. Systemic coagulopathy follows over the subsequent hours, consistent with the hemotoxic classification this species carries in regional snakebite frameworks.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Local tissue effects (swelling, blistering, necrosis risk) combined with venom-induced consumption coagulopathy and systemic bleeding — the same general hemotoxic viper picture seen elsewhere on this site, occurring here in one of the region's most frequently encountered venomous snakes.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Because this species has a documented behavioral tendency to remain near the bite location rather than retreat, there's a real secondary-bite risk to bystanders or rescuers attempting to identify or move the snake — leave that to trained personnel.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial coagulation studies and limb assessment per standard hemotoxic viper protocol.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Purified monovalent equine antivenin is manufactured locally in Thailand (Thai Red Cross Society, Queen Saovabha Memorial Institute) specifically for this species, alongside the country's other medically important snakes. This is a well-supported, well-supplied antivenom situation relative to several other entries on this site — competent treatment is described as widely available throughout Thailand, contributing to serious morbidity being far more common than death in the country's modern snakebite data.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation monitoring and wound care per standard viper protocol.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Volume matters here more than exotic severity — this is the single largest contributor to Thailand's snakebite burden, so competence with this species specifically has outsized practical value in the region compared with rarer but more dramatic entries elsewhere on this page.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Redback Spider
items.html: (Latrodectus hasselti — Australia's relative of the North American black widow) — intense local, radiating, and sometimes generalized pain with sweating; not life-threatening, and no confirmed death since antivenom was introduced in 1956. Care: standard analgesia is first-line; two placebo-controlled RCTs (RAVE, RAVE-II) found antivenom no better than placebo for pain or systemic effects, so routine antivenom use is now discouraged in Australian guidance — reserve it for severe pain unresponsive to analgesics. Do NOT use pressure immobilization here — unlike funnel-web, this venom acts slowly and PBI tends to worsen local pain rather than help.

items.name: White-Tailed Spider
items.html: (Lampona spp.) — the "flesh-eating bite" reputation is a thoroughly debunked myth; a prospective study of 130 confirmed bites found zero cases of necrotic ulcers. Care: ice for pain, reassurance; no antibiotics or debridement indicated on this basis alone.

regions.label: South Asia
regions.lede: The "Big Four" — the four species responsible for the overwhelming majority of snakebite morbidity and mortality across India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Nepal. All four are covered by a single Indian polyvalent antivenom, but that coverage is meaningfully uneven across the region given real venom variation between populations. Two additional critical species round out this page precisely because they fall outside that framework — one with no working antivenom, one where antivenom isn't even the primary treatment.

species.search: russell's viper daboia russelii russell viper
species.title: Russell's Viper
species.subtitle: Daboia russelii. The single most medically important snake in South Asia — India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar. Responsible for over half of India's snakebite deaths

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling develop promptly at the bite site. Coagulopathy, renal dysfunction, and (in South Indian and Sri Lankan populations specifically) neuromuscular paralysis can all follow — this species doesn't stay in one mechanism lane the way most vipers do.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Local swelling, coagulopathy (VICC), acute kidney injury, and myonecrosis are the core picture. Sri Lankan and South Indian Russell's viper populations additionally cause a distinct neuromuscular paralysis not typically seen with other regional Daboia populations — ptosis and other cranial nerve findings can develop alongside the hemotoxic picture. Abdominal pain has been identified as an early feature of systemic envenoming in Sri Lankan data, appearing before more obvious bleeding signs — worth treating as a red flag rather than a nonspecific complaint.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. No tourniquet, incision, or suction.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Baseline and serial coagulation studies, renal function, and urinalysis. A 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) is the standard regional bedside screen — recheck roughly 6 hours after antivenom, since that's the approximate time needed for the liver to replenish consumed clotting factors. Watch closely for evolving renal injury independent of the coagulopathy picture.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by Indian polyvalent antivenom (VINS, Bharat, and other manufacturers), raised against all "Big Four" species — but sourced predominantly from Tamil Nadu (South India) venom. This matters clinically: documented venom composition differences across Daboia populations mean the same antivenom performs less reliably against Sri Lankan, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi Russell's vipers than against South Indian ones. Dosing protocols vary by country and product concentration rather than a single universal number — commonly an initial dose followed by reassessment against the 20WBCT and clinical picture, with escalation for persistent coagulopathy. Antivenom reliably clears free venom from the bloodstream but does NOT reliably reverse neurotoxicity that has already developed — this is a distinct failure mode from the coagulopathy response, which does respond well.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation and renal monitoring regardless of initial severity, given the AKI risk. Any neuromuscular signs warrant the same airway vigilance as a primarily neurotoxic bite.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't assume "polyvalent antivenom" means uniform coverage across the region — a Sri Lankan, Pakistani, or Bangladeshi patient may respond less predictably to an Indian-manufactured product raised against South Indian venom than the label alone would suggest. Renal injury can evolve on its own trajectory separate from the coagulopathy — track it independently, not just as a coagulopathy complication.

species.search: common krait bungarus caeruleus indian krait blue krait
species.title: Common Krait
species.subtitle: Bungarus caeruleus. Also called: Indian krait, blue krait. Nocturnal, painless bite — often called the "silent killer" because victims frequently don't realize they've been bitten until paralysis sets in overnight

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Bites classically occur indoors at night, on people sleeping on the floor. The bite itself is often painless, with minimal or no visible local findings — victims commonly wake with symptoms already progressing, or don't wake at all until paralysis is advanced. Progression to respiratory paralysis can occur within hours.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Descending neuromuscular paralysis: ptosis progressing to complete ophthalmoplegia, facial and bulbar weakness, neck weakness, and ultimately respiratory failure. Abdominal pain is a recognized early feature. Critically, this is a bite with essentially no local tissue signs — no significant swelling or necrosis — which is itself a diagnostic clue when the biting snake wasn't seen or identified.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Maintain high suspicion in anyone found with unexplained paralysis or altered consciousness after sleeping on the floor in an endemic area, even without a clear bite history. Rapid transport; airway monitoring en route.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Antivenom clears free venom from the blood but does not reliably reverse paralysis that has already developed — patients can progress to needing intubation despite timely, appropriately dosed antivenom. Don't interpret ongoing paralysis after antivenom as treatment failure requiring more antivenom; it often reflects venom already bound at the neuromuscular junction. Have ventilator support ready and do not delay intubation for respiratory compromise while waiting to see if other measures work.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by Indian polyvalent antivenom. The regional national protocol includes a neostigmine/atropine trial (atropine first to blunt cholinergic side effects, then neostigmine) in many centers, but the evidence for krait specifically is genuinely mixed: at least one prospective study of 72 confirmed krait-bite patients found zero clinical improvement from neostigmine, with all patients progressing to respiratory paralysis regardless. Other case reports describe a "neostigmine responsiveness test" identifying a subset of patients who do improve. Given the low downside and established regional protocol, a trial is reasonable, but it should never delay or substitute for ventilatory support when respiratory compromise is present.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: ICU-level care with ventilator availability for any patient with neurologic signs. Recovery can be prolonged — case reports describe over a week of mechanical ventilation with eventual full recovery, so a slow response doesn't necessarily mean a poor prognosis.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: The painless, sign-free bite is the whole danger here — treat any unexplained overnight paralysis in an endemic area as a krait bite until proven otherwise, particularly if the patient was sleeping at floor level. Don't wait on neostigmine response before securing the airway.

species.search: indian cobra naja naja spectacled cobra
species.title: Indian Cobra
species.subtitle: Naja naja. Also called: spectacled cobra. Common in both rural and urban/peri-urban settings across the subcontinent

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Unlike krait, local pain and swelling at the bite site are typically apparent early — this is a useful bedside differentiator between the two elapids when the snake wasn't identified. Neurotoxic progression follows a similar descending pattern to krait but the venom is generally considered less potent milligram-for-milligram.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Combines neurotoxic descending paralysis (ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar and respiratory weakness) with real local cytotoxic tissue effects — swelling, blistering, and potential local necrosis at the bite site, which krait does not typically produce.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard elapid approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Local wound care as findings warrant.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Same airway vigilance as any neurotoxic elapid bite. Local wound monitoring for necrosis/secondary infection, distinct from the pure neurotoxic-only picture of krait.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered by Indian polyvalent antivenom. Some regional protocols and case data suggest neostigmine has more consistent benefit in cobra bites than in krait bites specifically, though this should still be treated as an adjunct rather than a substitute for antivenom and ventilatory readiness.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for airway monitoring and wound care. Ventilator availability for any respiratory signs, as with krait.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Local necrosis and tissue findings are the key bedside clue distinguishing this from a krait bite when the snake is unidentified — a painful, swollen bite with neurologic signs points here; a painless, sign-free bite with new paralysis points to krait.

species.search: saw-scaled viper echis carinatus india pakistan carpet viper
species.title: Saw-Scaled Viper
species.subtitle: Echis carinatus. Smallest of the Big Four but disproportionately dangerous given how common bites are — high local abundance across India and Pakistan in particular. A distinct population from the Middle Eastern Echis coloratus/carinatus covered on that region's page

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local pain and swelling within minutes, with coagulopathy developing over the following hours.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy driving systemic bleeding, alongside local pain, swelling, and occasional tissue necrosis at the bite site.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: 20WBCT and serial coagulation studies, same framework as Russell's viper.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Covered directly by Indian polyvalent antivenom — this is one of the four species the product is raised against, so coverage here is more consistent than for some of the region's other medically significant but non-Big-Four species.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation monitoring per standard viper protocol.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Don't confuse regional Echis populations — a product effective against South Asian E. carinatus is not automatically interchangeable with antivenom for African or Middle Eastern Echis species (see the Africa and Middle East pages); the reverse also holds. This is one of the more consistent narrow-cross-reactivity teaching points across the whole Echis genus.

species.search: hump-nosed pit viper hypnale hypnale merrem's hump-nosed viper
species.title: Hump-Nosed Pit Viper
species.subtitle: Hypnale hypnale (plus H. zara and H. nepa, endemic to Sri Lanka). Not part of the "Big Four" by tradition, but a genuinely major cause of snakebite in its range — and the standard antivenom does not work against it

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Local swelling develops early in the large majority of bites. Blood incoagulability can appear anywhere from 15 minutes to 48 hours after the bite, and in most cases is already present by the time the patient reaches hospital.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: In the largest published Sri Lankan series (302 confirmed bites), local swelling occurred in 91% and local necrosis in 16%, with 4% requiring digit amputation and 4% needing skin grafts. Venom-induced consumption coagulopathy was detected in 39%, spontaneous systemic bleeding in 18%, and acute renal failure in 10% — with an overall case fatality rate of 1.7%. This is a genuinely small snake causing disproportionate morbidity: it was the single most common identified snakebite species in that series, ahead of every other snake in the country.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Standard viper approach: immobilize, remove constricting items, transport. Bites most commonly occur on the feet or ankles at night near people's homes — a distinct epidemiological pattern worth recognizing.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Serial coagulation studies and renal function monitoring, same framework as other regional vipers. Given the real necrosis and amputation risk seen in the case series, involve surgical/wound care early for significant local findings rather than treating this as a purely medical-management bite.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: This is the critical point: the standard Indian polyvalent antivenoms used across South Asia (including Bharat and Haffkine products) have been clinically and laboratory-confirmed to be NOT effective against Hypnale venom — this snake is not one of the four species the standard product is raised against, despite historically being misidentified as Russell's viper or saw-scaled viper in many cases, which likely contributed to years of under-recognition. No antivenom is currently available in India for this species. In Sri Lanka, some case reports and lab studies suggest cross-neutralization from Thai Red Cross products (Malayan pit viper monovalent, or Hemato polyvalent), but this is not a standardized, widely available clinical solution — management remains predominantly supportive.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit for coagulation and renal monitoring regardless of antivenom availability, given the real fatality and complication rates in confirmed bites. Supportive management — fluid/electrolyte correction, transfusion support for significant bleeding, dialysis if renal failure develops — is the mainstay rather than antivenom-centered care.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: This is arguably the single most important teaching point on this entire regional page: "give the polyvalent antivenom" is NOT the answer for this species, unlike every other South Asian viper covered here. A snake this genuinely common causing real mortality with no working antivenom is a distinct clinical reality from the Big Four framework — don't let the "Big Four" label create a false sense that it covers the region's full risk.

species.search: indian red scorpion hottentotta tamulus mesobuthus tamulus prazosin
species.regionTag: India, E. Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka
species.title: Indian Red Scorpion
species.subtitle: Hottentotta tamulus (formerly Mesobuthus/Buthus tamulus). Widely considered among the most dangerous scorpion species globally — not because of the sting itself, but because of the autonomic cascade it triggers

fields.label: Onset / Timeline
fields.html: Intense local pain at the sting site is immediate. Systemic autonomic effects follow over a period of hours: hypertension typically within 1-10 hours, tachycardia within 1-24 hours, and pulmonary edema — the feared complication — within 6-24 hours in published series.

fields.label: Clinical Syndrome
fields.html: Venom delays sodium channel inactivation and inhibits potassium channels, driving a massive, sustained catecholamine release — an "autonomic storm." Mild cases show vasoconstriction and hypertension; severe cases progress to hypotension, pulmonary edema, and myocardial dysfunction. Priapism has been specifically documented in pediatric case series. ECG changes are common — ST depression, tented T waves, an acute-infarction-like pattern — reflecting real myocardial stress rather than primary cardiac disease. Children are disproportionately represented among severe and fatal cases.

fields.label: Field / Prehospital Management
fields.html: Immobilize the affected limb and transport urgently — early treatment is the single most important factor in preventing progression to pulmonary edema. Do not delay for traditional or non-medical remedies; delayed presentation is a repeatedly documented factor in severe outcomes.

fields.label: ED / Resuscitation Management
fields.html: Recognize this as a cardiovascular emergency, not primarily a pain management problem. Serial vital signs and ECG monitoring given the real risk of evolving pulmonary edema and myocardial dysfunction over the following 24 hours.

fields.label: Antivenom
fields.html: Scorpion antivenom has shown limited clinical benefit for this species specifically and is not the primary treatment. Prazosin (an oral post-synaptic alpha-1 blocker) is the treatment that has changed outcomes here — in a landmark comparative study, mortality was 25% with conventional therapy, 3.5% with nifedipine, and 0% with prazosin; complicating pulmonary edema fell from 46% to zero across the same comparison. For prazosin-resistant cardiotoxicity, dobutamine has shown benefit in case series. Severe pulmonary edema unresponsive to first-line measures has been managed with sodium nitroprusside or inotropic support in published cases.

fields.label: Disposition
fields.html: Admit any patient with systemic signs for cardiovascular monitoring — this applies especially to children, who show higher rates of severe complications. Even patients presenting late (one published case: 36 hours, with established pulmonary edema) have recovered with prazosin and supportive care, so a delayed presentation is not itself a reason to withhold treatment.

pearls.label: Pearls / Pitfalls
pearls.html: Prazosin is the single highest-yield intervention for this species and is inexpensive, widely available, and free of the anaphylaxis risk that comes with antivenom — this is genuinely one of the best-supported low-cost antidotes on this entire site, backed by a striking mortality difference in comparative data. Don't reflexively reach for antivenom as the primary answer here the way you would with most other critical entries on this page.

nonCritical.label: Non-Critical — Supportive Care Only
nonCritical.sub: Not life-threatening and doesn't require antivenom or critical-care intervention. Not a full workup — just enough to recognize and reassure.

items.name: Green Vine Snake
items.html: (Ahaetulla nasuta and related species) — mildly venomous, rear-fanged; bites cause local swelling and mild pain only, no reported systemic envenoming of significance. Care: wound cleaning and reassurance; no antivenom exists or is needed.

items.name: Non-Venomous Mimics
items.html: (rat snake, wolf snake, checkered keelback, and others) — frequently mistaken for the Big Four given overlapping habitat and superficial resemblance, causing significant patient and family anxiety. Care: confirm species when possible (photo, description, or expert identification); wound care only, no antivenom, no coagulation workup needed once a non-venomous species is confirmed.
